metadata.title: Fake Elon Musk Stream Drew 500,000 Viewers as Coinbase AI Blocked $4.7M in Crypto Transfers

content.text:
Key Takeaways
-
A fake Tesla livestream used an AI-generated Elon Musk to promise viewers it would double any crypto they sent.
-
Coinbase says its automated defenses stopped $4.7 million from leaving customer accounts.
-
Customers approved the transfers themselves, exposing a blind spot in defenses designed to detect account takeovers.
Coinbase says its AI fraud defenses stopped $4.7 million in crypto transfers to scammers who used an Elon Musk deepfake to promote a fake Tesla giveaway on YouTube.
The livestream drew more than 500,000 viewers, according to the exchange.
Coinbase said hundreds of its customers attempted to send crypto to the scammers over roughly two hours.
Fake Elon Musk Tesla Giveaway
In its Nov. 17 disclosure, Coinbase said the scammers made their stream appear to be an official broadcast of Tesla's flying-car demonstration.
An AI-generated Musk promised to double any crypto viewers sent, while the broadcast displayed wallet addresses and a QR code.
The giveaway had already convinced customers by the time they reached Coinbase's confirmation screen.
They approved the transfers from their own accounts, making the payments harder to distinguish from legitimate activity.
"Our systems can see risk signals in real time. They can't see intent," Coinbase wrote.
How Coinbase Used AI to Interrupt the Scam
Coinbase said its machine-learning models screened transfers in real time for signs of fraud, including brand impersonation and payments to recently created wallet addresses.
When a transfer raised a flag, an automated agent could ask the customer about the offer in what Coinbase called a "short, targeted conversation."
It could then explain why being asked to send crypto upfront in exchange for twice as much was a sign of fraud.
Coinbase said the system scored each reply before showing it to the customer and handled the interventions "with no humans in the loop."
Elon Musk and Ripple Deepfakes Have Pushed Similar Giveaways
In June 2024, scammers hijacked Australian broadcaster 7News' YouTube channel and used an AI-generated Musk to promote a crypto scam.
CCN reported that the broadcasts reached more than 100,000 people.
Ripple warned of a similar scheme in July 2025 after deepfakes of CEO Brad Garlinghouse appeared on YouTube promising to double viewers' XRP.
The videos revived a scam Ripple had already taken YouTube to court over in 2020.
The companies settled the following year.
